questions.q: Per this lesson's methodology, what should you determine before touching a single query or index?
options: Whether the problem affects one query or the whole system, whether it's a new regression or has always been slow, and what SQL Server is actually waiting on
Nothing -- you should immediately rewrite whatever query the user complained about
Only whether the server has enough disk space
Whether the database is on Azure SQL Database or Managed Instance
questions.explain: Scope, timing, and wait stats form the triage order this lesson establishes before reaching for any specific tuning tool.

questions.q: Why check wait stats before reading an execution plan or adding an index?
options: The wait type tells you which category of problem you're dealing with -- e.g. a PAGEIOLATCH wait means disk I/O, not a missing index, and an LCK_M wait means blocking, not a bad plan
Wait stats are only useful for Azure SQL Managed Instance, not other deployment types
Execution plans can't be read until wait stats are cleared
Wait stats replace the need to ever look at an execution plan
questions.explain: Skipping this step is how DBAs waste time tuning a query or index that was never the actual bottleneck.

questions.q: What's the difference between a query that's a 'new regression' versus one that has 'always been slow', per this lesson?
options: A regression means a good plan got replaced by a worse one (often after a statistics update or parameter sniffing); always-slow more often means the query never had a good plan or index to begin with
There is no meaningful difference between the two
A regression can only happen on Azure SQL Database, never on-prem
Always-slow queries are never fixable
questions.explain: Query Store (Lessons 48-49) is built specifically to answer this question by keeping plan history over time.

questions.q: Which DMV shows instance-wide cumulative wait time by wait type?
options: sys.dm_os_wait_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.dm_exec_sql_text
sys.dm_db_missing_index_details
questions.explain: sys.dm_exec_requests shows what one live session is waiting on right now; sys.dm_os_wait_stats is the instance-wide, cumulative view.

questions.q: A query is reported as slow, and CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER is the top wait type for that session. What does that point to?
options: Parallelism between worker threads, not disk I/O and not blocking
A missing index that must be created immediately
A hardware failure on the storage subsystem
A deadlock that has already killed the session
questions.explain: The wait-type crib sheet in this lesson maps CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER specifically to parallelism, distinct from PAGEIOLATCH (I/O) and LCK_M (blocking).
